task.passage: These arrangements, which had won the admiration of all the critics, were put into execution on 3 Vendemiaire, Year VIII (25 September 1799), at five in the morning. Preparations for the crossing had been made near the village of Dietikon with extraordinary care and secrecy. Boats had been dragged by hand and hidden in the woods. By morning they were afloat, and the troops were silently drawn up on the bank. General Foy, later distinguished as an orator, commanded the artillery in this memorable battle; he positioned several batteries to protect the crossing. Six hundred men boldly embarked and reached the opposite bank. They immediately attacked and scattered the enemy skirmishers. Korsakoff had stationed three battalions with artillery there, on the plateau of Closter-Fahr. Our artillery, skilfully directed, soon silenced the Russian guns and protected the successive crossings of our advance guard. When General Gazan had assembled sufficient reinforcements with the six hundred men who had crossed first, he advanced against the three Russian battalions guarding Closter-Fahr. They had established themselves in a wood and defended it bravely. Gazan surrounded them and had to kill almost every last man to dislodge them. Once these three battalions had been destroyed, the bridge was laid. The rest of Lorge's division and part of Mesnard's division crossed the Limmat: fifteen thousand men had been brought across the river. Bontemps's brigade was stationed at Regensdorf to face Durasof should he move up from the lower Limmat. The main body, directed by chief of staff Oudinot, moved upstream along the Limmat to reach the rear of Zurich.
task.question: Immediately after their initial boat crossing, where did the first six hundred French soldiers land, before Gazan assembled further reinforcements?

task.passage: Once this part of the operation was completed, Massena personally returned to the other bank of the Limmat to oversee the movements of his wings. On the lower Limmat, Mesnard had so thoroughly deceived Durasof with his demonstrations that the latter had moved to the bank and opened fire with all his guns. On his right, Mortier had advanced towards Zurich by way of Wollishofen, but had encountered Korsakoff's main force, positioned, as already stated, in front of the Limmat, and had been compelled to fall back. Arriving at that moment, Massena set Klein's division, which was at Altstetten, in motion. Humbert, at the head of his four thousand grenadiers, marched on Zurich and restored the battle. Mortier renewed his attacks, and the Russians were thus confined within Zurich.
task.question: Where was Klein's division stationed immediately before Massena set it in motion, rather than where Humbert subsequently marched?

task.passage: Korsakoff had finally realized his situation and had moved his troops into the other part of Zurich, behind the Limmat. Durasof, on the lower Limmat, had slipped away on learning of the crossing; avoiding Bontemps's brigade by a detour, he had regained the road to Vintherthur. The next day, 4 Vendemiaire (26 September), the fighting was to be fierce, for the Russians wanted to force a way out and the French wanted to take great spoils. Fighting began early. The unfortunate city of Zurich, crowded with artillery, baggage and wounded men and attacked from every side, seemed enveloped in fire. On this side of the Limmat, Mortier and Klein had reached the city and were about to enter it. Beyond the river, Oudinot pressed it from the rear and sought to block Korsakoff's route. This road to Vintherthur, the scene of bloody fighting, had been taken and retaken several times. Finally deciding to withdraw, Korsakoff placed his infantry at the head, his cavalry in the centre, and his artillery and baggage at the rear. He advanced in this way in a long column. His brave infantry, charging furiously, swept everything before it and opened a passage; but after it had passed with part of the cavalry, the French charged again, attacked the remaining cavalry and baggage, and drove them back to the gates of Zurich. At the same moment, Klein and Mortier entered from their side. Fighting took place in the streets. The renowned and unfortunate Lavater was struck at the door of his house by a bullet fired by a drunken Swiss soldier who had put his musket to his chest to demand money; he fell with a serious wound to his thigh, from which he died some months later. Finally, all those who had remained in Zurich were forced to lay down their arms. One hundred cannon, all the baggage, the administrative services, the army treasury and five thousand prisoners fell into French hands. Korsakoff had also had eight thousand men put out of action in this bitter struggle. Eight and five made thirteen thousand men lost, that is, half his army. The great battles in Italy had produced no more extraordinary results. The consequences for the rest of the campaign were to be no less important than the material gains. Korsakoff, with at most thirteen thousand men, hastened back to the Rhine.
task.question: After Korsakoff recognized his predicament and moved his troops, but before the fighting described for the next morning, in which part of Zurich relative to the Limmat were his troops now positioned?
